# Toric ideals are generated by binomials

Let $X$ be a set of cells, possibly infinite, and let $T$ assign to each cell $x$ a finitely
supported exponent vector $T(x) \in \mathbb{N}^{(J)}$, for a set $J$ of parameters. Tables of counts
are finitely supported maps $X \to \mathbb{N}$, moves are finitely supported maps
$X \to \mathbb{Z}$, and the sufficient statistic of a table $a$ is $T(a) = \sum_x a(x)\, T(x)$. For
a field $k$, $k[X]$ is the polynomial ring in the variables $x \in X$, $x^a = \prod_x x^{a(x)}$ for
a table $a$, and the toric ideal $I_T$ is the kernel of the monomial map
$k[X] \to k[t_j : j \in J]$, $x \mapsto t^{T(x)}$. Over every field $k$, the toric ideal $I_T$ is
the ideal generated by the binomials $x^a - x^b$ with $T(a) = T(b)$.

This is the first stage of the proof of Theorem 3.1 of Diaconis and Sturmfels, where the binomials
are written as $x^{f^+} - x^{f^-}$ with $\sum_x f(x)\, T(x) = 0$; the two generating sets agree up
to monomial factors. The paper argues with a leading-term induction. Grouping the terms of a
polynomial by the fibre of their exponents shows more: every polynomial of $I_T$ is a $k$-linear
combination of such binomials.

## Sources

- P. Diaconis and B. Sturmfels, *Algebraic algorithms for sampling from conditional distributions*, Ann. Statist. 26 (1998), 363–397, Section 3.1, proof of Theorem 3.1.
